problem: The skin depths 'At 50 Hz, steel δ is centimetres; at 10 kHz it is a few millimetres' are true only for steel with μ_r ≈ 1 (above the Curie point or austenitic). For magnetic steel at room temperature (μ_r ≈ 100, ρ ≈ 2 × 10⁻⁷ Ω·m) the same formula gives δ ≈ 3 mm at 50 Hz and ≈ 0.23 mm at 10 kHz — exactly the value quiz Q3 computes. A student who does Q3 and then reads 'a few millimetres at 10 kHz' sees a contradiction.
fix: State the permeability assumed with each figure, e.g.: 'Above the Curie point steel is non-magnetic (μ_r ≈ 1, ρ ≈ 1 × 10⁻⁶ Ω·m): δ ≈ 7 cm at 50 Hz and ≈ 5 mm at 10 kHz. Magnetic steel at room temperature (μ_r ≈ 100, ρ ≈ 2 × 10⁻⁷ Ω·m) gives δ ≈ 3 mm at 50 Hz and ≈ 0.2 mm at 10 kHz.' Add the same assumption to exam trap 1.

problem: 'Power drops unless the control raises frequency or DC link voltage' conflicts with Section 2, which says that above resonance moving f closer to resonance raises power, so raising f lowers it. Above the Curie point the coil inductance falls, so the tank's resonant frequency rises and the old operating frequency ends up below resonance; the remedy is to follow the new resonance, not simply to raise f.
fix: Above the Curie point μ_r falls to about 1, so δ grows, R_ref falls and hysteresis loss disappears. The coil inductance L falls, the tank resonant frequency rises, and the inverter must raise its frequency to stay at resonance; power is then restored by raising the DC-link voltage (or by longer on-time), not by detuning further.
